evidence_quotes.quote: Here, we assessed health risks from consumption of contaminated well water on the Crow Reservation by conducting a community-engaged, cumulative risk assessment. Well water testing, surveys and interviews were used to collect data on contaminant concentrations, water treatment methods, well water consumption, and well and septic system protection and maintenance practices.
Although 15% of the US population (49 million people) rely on private wells, the federal government does not regulate home well water quality

Additionally, lack of community health education about well maintenance and well water safety, pre-existing health conditions such as diabetes, and limited environmental enforcement increase community vulnerability.

evidence_quotes.quote: Despite widespread poor well water quality, almost no one uses water treatment technology. Comparing water quality data with survey data shows that although 77% of all wells tested have unacceptably hard water (above the EPA SMCL), only 3.3% of families had installed a water softener.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household drinking and cooking water from private domestic wells among rural Crow Reservation families, including access to safe and palatable drinking water, household treatment adoption, reliance on hauled and bottled water, and affordability barriers.
criterion_notes.c2: Fails both the plain wording and the 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading of Criterion 2. Under the plain wording, the study does not empirically examine a legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory, or governance factor: its empirical exposure is inorganic contamination of private domestic well water alongside household socioeconomic and environmental health literacy factors. EPA MCLs, SMCLs, Health Advisories, and Reference Doses are used solely as numerical toxicological and palatability benchmarks for risk calculation, while mentions that private wells are federally unregulated, that state laws do not apply on reservation trust lands, and (citing external literature) that limited environmental enforcement and jurisdictional complexity contribute to disparities appear only as unanalysed background context and policy recommendations. Under the 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading, no rule-type mechanism directly governing service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, tenure/documentation rules, tariffs, discretion, enforcement actions, or utility regulatory structure) is analysed.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary empirical data from a mixed-methods CBPR study: laboratory water-quality testing of 164 domestic wells, comparison with ~650 historical Indian Health Service well records, a survey of 197 adults across 165 Tribal families, and qualitative interviews with 30 key informants.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports household safe-water availability, exclusion/avoidance due to contamination and unpalatability, treatment uptake, and affordability outcomes, including percentage of wells unsafe for lifetime consumption (39.2% non-carcinogenic HI > 1.0; 47.4% including arsenic cancer risk), proportion of households drinking/cooking with well water (80%) versus hauling all consumptive water (20%), household water-treatment use (3.3% water softeners, 4% reverse osmosis), reliance on bottled water (53%) or municipal sources (17%), and financial hardship of buying bottled water or treatment equipment.
criterion_notes.c5: Clearly identifies the population and unit of analysis (rural Crow Reservation households and domestic wells; 164 wells, 165 surveyed families/197 individuals, 30 interviewees), chemical/water-quality exposures, risk and household water-use/coping outcomes, and cross-sectional mixed-methods CBPR study design.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is published in English.

study_design: Cross-sectional mixed-methods community-based participatory research (CBPR) cumulative risk assessment combining domestic well water quality testing, secondary well records, household surveys, and qualitative key-informant interviews
population_and_sample: Rural Apsaalooke (Crow) Tribal households relying on private domestic wells on the Crow Reservation, Montana (164 domestic wells tested; 197 adult survey respondents from 165 families; 30 key informants interviewed; ~650 historical IHS well records)
exposure: Inorganic and microbial contaminants in private domestic well water (uranium, manganese, nitrate, zinc, arsenic, total dissolved solids, sulfate, iron, hardness, coliform/E. coli), alongside household financial constraints and well-stewardship literacy
outcome: Cumulative non-carcinogenic (Hazard Index) and carcinogenic health risk benchmarks, EPA MCL/SMCL exceedances, household well-water consumption versus avoidance (water hauling and bottled water purchase), household water-treatment adoption, and financial hardship of obtaining safe water
rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure). Although this empirical mixed-methods CBPR study examines rural Crow Reservation households' domestic well water safety, consumption, treatment adoption, water hauling, and financial barriers to safe drinking water, its empirical exposure is natural/anthropogenic inorganic well-water contamination (U, Mn, NO3-, Zn, As, TDS) and household socioeconomic/literacy factors rather than any legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory, or governance factor. Mentions of private wells being unregulated, state laws not applying on trust lands, and cited literature on limited environmental enforcement appear solely as unanalysed background context, failing Criterion 2 under both the plain wording and the 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading.
